name: marine-space-use
title: Marine megafauna space use
description: Tracked individuals per one-degree cell, 1985-2018, pooled across 121 species. Reflects research effort as much as animal distribution.
attribution: Sequeira, A. M. M. et al. (2025) Global tracking of marine megafauna space use reveals how to achieve conservation targets. Science. Data: https://doi.org/10.5061/dryad.x95x69ptv
caveats: Derived products only — 1-degree gridded space use, not raw tracks. Grid cell counts of tracked individuals reflect research effort as much as animal distribution; the published bias-testing datasets must be used alongside them. Covers 1985–2018, so it does not speak to the last several years.

name: aerial-passage
title: Nightly aerial passage
description: Weekly median of nightly reflectivity traffic past US weather radars, pooled across 1995-2025, with each station's shift in autumn passage date. Aerial biomass, not birds: the radar does not separate birds from bats from insects. The autumn window is a northern-hemisphere one, so the shift means little at the tropical stations.
attribution: Dark Ecology project (2026). Dark Ecology Dataset: Measurements of Biological Activity in US Weather Radar — Time Series Data from 1995–2025, v1.1.0. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18433334
caveats: Measures aerial biomass, not birds: MistNet separates precipitation from biology, not birds from bats from insects. `traffic` is vertically and temporally integrated, so it carries no height information — use the profiles product for flight altitude. Station histories are uneven across 1995–2025 and the NEXRAD dual-polarisation upgrade around 2011–2013 is a step change in the instrument that must be modelled as a break rather than read as a biological trend; the daily product does not label hardware generation, so upgrade dates have to come from elsewhere. Nights with a high `fraction_missing` must be excluded before computing passage quantiles.
